title: Britain’s budget chose defence over energy bills
gist: Column arguing that chancellor John Healey's first budget and the approval of the Jackdaw gas field do little to cut UK energy bills — the January 2027 price cap is still forecast to rise 27% — while cuts of £720m to the boiler upgrade scheme and £100m to heat networks undermine the heat-pump transition, effectively prioritising defence spending over long-term bill reduction.

insights.claim: Energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh and chancellor John Healey confirmed approval of the Jackdaw gas field at Shell UK's Peterhead gas terminal while wearing Shell-branded high-vis jackets.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: Signals close government-industry alignment on North Sea gas; positive for Shell's UK upstream.
insights.locator: It was either a PR fail

insights.claim: Ministers contradicted each other on Jackdaw: Andy Burnham told parliament it would help with bills, while Fahnbulleh said it would not affect affordability or bills.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: Mixed government messaging; Jackdaw should not be priced in as a bill-reduction lever.
insights.quote: Jackdaw will not have an impact on affordability and bills
insights.locator: This was just one of a volley

insights.claim: The author argues Jackdaw and the larger Rosebank oil field have nothing to do with domestic energy bills and everything to do with geopolitical virtue signalling, with Donald Trump praising Burnham for 'getting it done'.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: UK North Sea approvals are partly driven by US alignment; watch Rosebank decision.
insights.locator: Jackdaw, and the even bigger Rosebank

insights.claim: According to the Office for Budget Responsibility, reopening Jackdaw only slows the decline of depleted North Sea reserves from 14 per cent a year to 10 per cent, and could create just 27 new jobs.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: North Sea output decline continues regardless; limited macro or employment upside from new approvals.
insights.locator: Jackdaw, and the even bigger Rosebank

insights.claim: Even if both Jackdaw and Rosebank were drilled, together they would meet only 2 to 3 per cent of UK gas demand.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: UK remains structurally dependent on volatile imported gas.
insights.locator: Next, we actually use that cheap

insights.claim: Fossil fuel lobbyists secured 506 meetings with Labour ministers in the government's first year, with BP, Shell and Equinor accounting for a combined 100, according to Fossil Free Parliament.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: Industry access to ministers suggests continued favourable UK upstream policy.
insights.locator: Fossil fuel industry lobbyists secured

insights.claim: Healey's budget included a one-off £100 payment to households in council tax bands A to D in England at a cost of £2.6bn to the exchequer.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: Fiscal cost of bill support is material relative to its per-household impact.
insights.locator: The Jackdaw shot across the bows

insights.claim: The VAT cut on electricity bills was extended to July 2027, worth about £50, adding only three months beyond its planned April end.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: Short-term relief; watch the cliff edge in July 2027.
insights.locator: The Jackdaw shot across the bows

insights.claim: The budget moved green subsidy costs off gas bills into general taxation, but not off electricity bills, with timing unclear.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: Asymmetric levy treatment keeps electricity relatively expensive versus gas, slowing electrification.
insights.locator: The Jackdaw shot across the bows

insights.claim: The 'Energy Debt Circuit Breaker' targeted debt relief is expected to save bill-payers only around £30 by 2030.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: Marginal impact on household energy affordability.
insights.locator: The Jackdaw shot across the bows

insights.claim: Standing charges will be scrapped from the gas bills of 23m households by 2027, but Martin Lewis says the cost will shift to unit rates, adding about 1p per kWh, with 60% paying less and 40% more.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: Redistributive rather than bill-reducing; high-usage households lose.
insights.quote: About 60% of people will pay less due to this, 40% more.
insights.locator: Healey briefly put down the scattergun

insights.claim: The January 2027 energy price cap is still predicted to rise 27 per cent, from £1,723 to £2,192, an increase of £465, with confirmation expected on 25 November.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: Key date 25 November; rising bills squeeze UK consumer spending and inflation into 2027.
insights.locator: Another shot, then, that failed

themes.theme: Structural fix: decouple power from gas and electrify heat

insights.claim: UK energy bills are among Europe's highest because marginal cost pricing lets the most expensive generator, almost always gas, set the price for all electricity even when renewables are cheap.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: Electricity market reform (decoupling) is the main lever for lower UK power prices; watch government consultation.
insights.locator: How, then, do we reduce energy bills?

insights.claim: The government is still only 'seeking views' on decoupling electricity prices from gas, with no decision taken.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: Policy uncertainty persists for UK power-market reform.
insights.locator: How, then, do we reduce energy bills?

insights.claim: Around 80 per cent of UK households have a gas boiler, and new homes are still connected to the gas grid despite the Climate Change Committee's 2019 recommendation to end this by 2025.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: Large retrofit market remains untapped; policy slippage delays heat-pump demand.
insights.locator: Next, we actually use that cheap

insights.claim: The Climate Change Committee says heat pump installations must rise from around 60,000 in 2023 to nearly 450,000 by 2030 and 1.5m by 2035.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: Implied sevenfold growth target for UK heat-pump installers and manufacturers — now at risk.
insights.locator: Next, we actually use that cheap

insights.claim: The budget cut the boiler upgrade scheme by £720m and shifted from grants to low-interest loans, while heat network spending was cut by £100m this financial year.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: Negative for UK heat-pump and district-heating demand near term.
insights.locator: Here, one of Healey’s shots did

insights.claim: The Energy Saving Trust warned the cuts, together with about £1bn lost capital funding for the warm homes plan, risk sending the wrong message on low-carbon heat.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: Sector bodies expect weaker uptake of low-carbon heating.
insights.locator: The Energy Saving Trust responded

insights.claim: E3G's Ed Matthew called the cuts profoundly short-sighted, arguing they keep households hooked on high-cost gas, while Friends of the Earth's Mike Childs wants heat pumps funded by higher taxes on oil and gas firms.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: Pressure for windfall-style taxes on oil and gas remains a UK policy risk.
insights.quote: keep more households hooked on high-cost gas
insights.locator: The Energy Saving Trust responded

insights.claim: The author frames the budget as funding increased defence spending by cutting the warm homes budget while energy bills keep rising.
insights.speaker: Tim Smedley
insights.so_what: UK fiscal priority has shifted to defence at the expense of energy-transition spending.
insights.locator: Increasing defence spending by cutting
